# The Data Problem Is Bigger Than a Data Frame {#sec-problem}

A data frame can be perfectly valid R and still be the wrong input for a recurring delivery. The column names may have changed. A key may no longer be unique. A payment amount may be negative. A transformation may still run even though a downstream report no longer means what it meant last month.

This is the gap DataRaft addresses. It is not primarily a new way to manipulate rows. R and dplyr already do that well. It is a way to make the **delivery around the rows** explicit.

## A script is not an agreement

Consider a monthly policy file:

```{.r}
policies <- read.csv("policies.csv")
policies$premium <- round(policies$premium, 2)
summary(policies$premium)
```

The script says how to read and transform data. It does not say whether `policy_id` must exist, whether it must be unique, whether `premium` may be negative, who owns the definition, or what another process may rely on.

Those missing statements usually live elsewhere: in a notebook, a meeting, a ticket, a person's memory, or nowhere at all. As work becomes recurring, that omission creates predictable failure modes:

- schema changes are discovered only after downstream code fails;
- business rules are embedded in transformations instead of named checks;
- a successful run is confused with a valid delivery;
- a corrected rerun overwrites the context needed to explain the original result;
- consumers copy data because they cannot discover or trust a reusable product;
- ownership and expected service levels stay outside the executable workflow.

Logical data management literature frames the same problem at a larger scale: physical integration alone does not create a common logical understanding of data [@gardner2025logical]. DataRaft applies a narrower version of that idea inside an R-first workflow.

## The unit of work is the delivery

DataRaft's core abstraction is a `dr_product`. A product is a reusable specification, not the data itself. Current source code defines a product by identity, optional sources, preparation, a contract, quality rules, metadata, and an optional target. Execution produces a run result.

That distinction is important:

```text
product definition != data frame != run result != published release
```

A product can be inspected without reading data. A run can fail while the product definition remains valid. A successful run can remain only in memory. A published release adds a durable destination and evidence.

::: {.callout-important title="Mental model"}
Treat the product as the agreement about a recurring delivery. Treat a run as one attempt to satisfy that agreement.
:::

## Governance starts with explicit expectations

Governance in this book does not begin with a central catalog. It begins with simple executable statements:

- these columns are expected;
- these columns identify a row;
- these values must satisfy these rules;
- this definition has an owner;
- this output may be published only when its checks pass.

Later chapters add organization policies, output ports, service-level expectations, catalogs, and persistent release history. The early workflow does not require any of them.

## Why start locally

A common platform mistake is to introduce infrastructure before the team has a stable logical model. DataRaft intentionally permits an in-memory workflow with no database, object store, catalog service, Docker container, or cloud credential. That makes it possible to learn and test the governance semantics before choosing infrastructure.

This progression mirrors the teaching approach in *R for Data Science*: learn the whole game with a small working loop, then deepen each skill [@wickham2023r4ds]. We will follow the same rule throughout this book.

## Summary

A data platform is not just where data is stored. For recurring work, you also need executable expectations, named transformations, quality gates, evidence, and a path to publication. DataRaft makes those concerns composable around an R data product.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Open `data/policies.csv` and write down three assumptions you would want to be true every month. Do not write R code yet. Phrase each assumption as something a producer and consumer could both understand.
:::

## Exercises

1. Take one recurring R script you know. Write down three expectations that exist only in comments, tickets, or people's memory. Classify each as shape, business quality, ownership, or delivery behavior.
2. For the policy example, explain in one sentence why a data frame and a product definition are different objects even when they refer to the same columns.
3. Identify one situation where a plain script is still the right solution. What additional dependency would have to appear before a product abstraction becomes useful?
